provenance.other: “for Christ's sake” occurs in exactly three KJV verses (1 Corinthians 4:10, 2 Corinthians 12:10, Ephesians 4:32), and in none of them is the phrase continued. Only Romans 15:30 runs on as Jacob does — 'for the Lord Jesus Christ's sake, and for the love of the Spirit' — giving the five-word sequence 'Christ's sake, and for the' that Jacob completes with 'sake of our people'.
provenance.significance: Romans 15:30 is Paul asking a church to strive together with him in prayer; Jacob 1:4 is Jacob explaining what will be allowed onto a plate too small to hold a history. Both sentences name two beneficiaries of an effort, Christ first and a people second, in the same double construction. What the borrowing does to the colophon is make the criterion of selection apostolic rather than archival: the plates keep preaching, revelation and prophecy 'for Christ's sake, and for the sake of our people' because that is the pair Paul's request already assumes.

1:4.note: 'That I should engraven the heads of them upon these plates, and touch upon them as much as it were possible, for Christ's sake, and for the sake of our people.' The phrase 'for Christ's sake' occurs in exactly three KJV verses and stands alone in all of them; the doubled form Jacob uses, with 'and for the' following, is Romans 15:30's alone. This falls far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold for a quotation and is catalogued as an allusion accordingly — the evidence is the shape of the sequence, not its length.
1:4.text: Now I beseech you, brethren, for the Lord Jesus Christ’s sake, and for the love of the Spirit, that ye strive together with me in your prayers to God for me;

provenance.other: “what things should happen” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 10:32, where the object is 'unto him'. Jacob 1:5 has the same four words with 'unto them'. The parallel at Mark 10:32 in the other Synoptics does not use the construction.
provenance.significance: Recover the context and the borrowing supplies the chapter's whole argument. Mark 10:32 is the third passion prediction: Jesus takes the twelve apart on the road to Jerusalem to tell them 'what things should happen unto him', and the next verses are the betrayal, the mocking, the scourging and the killing. Jacob 1:5 has that clause for a revelation about his own people; 1:6 immediately says 'we knew of Christ and his Kingdom, which should come'; and 1:8 asks all men to 'view his death, and suffer his cross, and bear the shame of the world'. The one KJV verse behind Jacob's foreknowledge is Christ's foreknowledge of his own passion, and the three verses that follow it in Jacob are about exactly that.

1:5.note: 'It truly had been made manifest unto us concerning our people, what things should happen unto them.' A four-word KJV singleton, and the sense transfers cleanly: a private disclosure to a small group of what is coming. The link is proposed on rarity plus the sequence that follows it — Jacob moves from the disclosure (1:5) to knowing Christ (1:6) to viewing his death (1:8), which is the order of Mark 10:32-34.
1:5.text: And they were in the way going up to Jerusalem; and Jesus went before them: and they were amazed; and as they followed, they were afraid. And he took again the twelve, and began to tell them what things should happen unto him,

provenance.other: “the spirit of prophecy” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 19:10 — 'the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy'. Jacob 1:6 reads 'the spirit of much prophecy', which is the singleton with one word inserted.
provenance.significance: Revelation 19:10's clause is a definition, not a description: it identifies the spirit of prophecy with the testimony of Jesus. Jacob 1:6 says 'we also had many revelations, and the spirit of much prophecy; wherefore, we knew of Christ and his Kingdom, which should come' — and the 'wherefore' does what Revelation's copula does, deriving the knowledge of Christ from the spirit of prophecy. Neither verse argues the point; Revelation states it and Jacob infers from it.

1:6.note: 'And we also had many revelations, and the spirit of much prophecy.' The phrase is a KJV singleton, and Jacob's insertion of 'much' is the kind of adaptation the 1830 text makes freely. Catalogued as an echo rather than an allusion because four words with an interpolation is thin contact and the phrase had long since entered ordinary religious English; what recommends it is that Jacob's next clause performs the equation Revelation 19:10 makes.
1:6.text: And I fell at his feet to worship him. And he said unto me, See thou do it not: I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren that have the testimony of Jesus: worship God: for the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.

provenance.mt: Psalm 95:8 — 'Harden not your heart, as in the provocation, AND AS IN the day of temptation in the wilderness'; Psalm 95:11 — 'Unto whom I sware in MY wrath that they should not enter into MY rest.'
provenance.route: Psalm 95:8-11 via Hebrews 3:8-18 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The mediation is decided twice over, at two places where the KJV's psalm and the KJV's epistle differ. (1) “enter into his rest” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 3:18 — 'And to whom sware he that they should not enter into his rest' — which is the epistle's third-person recasting of the psalm's first-person 'into my rest'. “into my rest” occurs in exactly four KJV verses (Psalm 95:11, Hebrews 3:11, Hebrews 4:3, Hebrews 4:5). Jacob 1:7 has 'enter into his rest' and 'he should swear in his wrath', both third person, against the psalm's 'I sware in my wrath … my rest'. (2) Psalm 95:8 reads 'as in the provocation, AND AS IN the day of temptation'; Hebrews 3:8 drops 'and as' and reads 'as in the provocation, in the day of temptation'. Jacob reads 'as in the provocation in the days of temptation' — continuous, without the psalm's second 'as in'. “as in the provocation” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Psalm 95:8, Hebrews 3:8 and Hebrews 3:15, all of one text and its epistle. tools/mediation-check.py returns 'no decisive divergence' on both pairs, because its word alignment cannot register an ABSENCE (Hebrews' distinctive reading at 3:8 is the omission of 'and as') and because it compares only the two candidates named to it; the singleton count at 'enter into his rest' is what settles the case, and it settles it for Hebrews.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's spine and the pilot's kind of finding: a passage everyone reads as Psalm 95 turns out, at every point where the two testaments part, to have the epistle's wording. And the epistle's wording is not neutral. Psalm 95:11 is God's oath about a generation already dead; Hebrews 3-4 turns it into a live threat to its own readers, argues that the rest was never entered and remains open, and grounds the exhortation in 3:1's 'partakers of the heavenly calling' and 3:14's 'partakers of Christ'. Jacob 1:7 has that too — 'partake of the goodness of God' — and its purpose clause, persuading a people to come to Christ so that they may enter the rest they might otherwise be sworn out of, is Hebrews' argument in one sentence rather than the psalm's. The 'lest by any means' that governs the threat is likewise Pauline: it occurs in exactly three KJV verses, 1 Corinthians 8:9, 2 Corinthians 11:3 and Galatians 2:2.
provenance.alternative: Psalm 95:8-11 is the ultimate source and Hardy's apparatus names it first; the claim here is only about which English wording is being followed, not about which text is being remembered.

1:7.note: 'That they might enter into his rest, lest by any means he should swear in his wrath they should not enter in, as in the provocation in the days of temptation, while the children of Israel were in the wilderness.' Hardy's cross-references at this verse are Psalm 95:8, Hebrews 3:8, Psalm 95:8-11 and, for the underlying episodes, Exodus 17:1-7 and Numbers 20:2-13 — the waters of Massah and Meribah, which Exodus 17:7 names for the chiding and the tempting. What this catalogue adds is the mediation. Jacob has the New Testament form at both points of divergence: 'enter into his rest' rather than 'into my rest', which occurs in exactly one KJV verse and that verse is Hebrews 3:18; and 'as in the provocation in the days of temptation' run continuously, without the 'and as' that Psalm 95:8 interposes and Hebrews 3:8 removes. The 1830 'days' for Hebrews' 'day' is Jacob's own, and 1920 did not correct it.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Jacob 1.7 (Psalm 95:8; Hebrews 3:8; Psalm 95:8-11; Exodus 17:1-7; Numbers 20:2-13)
1:7.text: Harden not your hearts, as in the provocation, in the day of temptation in the wilderness:

provenance.other: “the children of Israel were in the wilderness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Numbers 15:32. Jacob 1:7 closes with the whole of it, conjunction included: 'while the children of Israel were in the wilderness'. Hebrews 3:8, which supplies the rest of the sentence, ends at 'in the wilderness' and does not name Israel.
provenance.significance: The clause is a gloss: Hebrews 3:8 says only 'in the wilderness', and Jacob adds the subject from the one KJV verse that has it. What that verse then contains is a wilderness provocation of its own — the man found gathering sticks on the sabbath, brought to Moses, and stoned by the whole congregation at the Lord's word (Numbers 15:32-36). So a sentence warning a people not to be sworn out of God's rest ends by quoting the setting of the KJV's sharpest wilderness punishment, and the eight words that fill out Hebrews' geography carry a story of a congregation executing one of its own for refusing rest on the day appointed for it.

1:7.note: 'As in the provocation in the days of temptation, while the children of Israel were in the wilderness.' An eight-word KJV singleton, and its position is exactly where Hebrews 3:8 stops. Confidence is moderate rather than high because the string is a natural way to say an ordinary thing and the writer had every reason to name Israel here whether or not Numbers 15:32 was in view; the case rests on the fact that the KJV says it in this order in one place only, and on the subject matter of that place.
1:7.text: And while the children of Israel were in the wilderness, they found a man that gathered sticks upon the sabbath day.

provenance.other: “would to God” occurs in exactly six KJV verses (Exodus 16:3, Joshua 7:7, Judges 9:29, Acts 26:29, 1 Corinthians 4:8, 2 Corinthians 11:1). In five of them the wish is a complaint or a piece of sarcasm — that Israel had died in Egypt, that they had dwelt beyond Jordan, that Paul's readers really did reign. Acts 26:29 is the only KJV verse in which the wish is that other people were Christians, and it is spoken in immediate answer to a sentence about persuasion.
provenance.significance: Agrippa says 'Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian', and Paul answers 'I would to God, that not only thou, but also all that hear me this day, were both almost, and altogether such as I am, except these bonds.' Jacob 1:8 puts the two halves back together: 'we would to God that we could persuade all men … that all men would believe in Christ.' The persuasion Agrippa declines and the wish Paul makes over him are one sentence in Jacob, and what Paul wishes them into — 'such as I am, except these bonds' — Jacob spells out as viewing his death, suffering his cross, and bearing the shame of the world. Paul's exception for his chains is precisely what Jacob refuses to except.

1:8.note: 'Wherefore, we would to God that we could persuade all men not to rebel against God … but that all men would believe in Christ.' The wish and the persuading belong together in exactly one KJV place, Acts 26:28-29, and Jacob has both, in Paul's order and with Paul's universal extension ('all that hear me this day' / 'all men'). Confidence is held at moderate because 'would to God' occurs in exactly six KJV verses and had long been ordinary English; the argument is the collocation with persuasion and belief in Christ, not the idiom.
1:8.text: And Paul said, I would to God, that not only thou, but also all that hear me this day, were both almost, and altogether such as I am, except these bonds.

provenance.route: Hebrews 12:2 (the pairing) + Ezekiel 34:29 (the wording of 'bear the shame') → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “endured the cross” and “despising the shame” each occur in exactly one KJV verse, and it is the same verse, Hebrews 12:2: the cross and the shame are joined nowhere else in the KJV. The wording of Jacob's second clause is Ezekiel's, however — “bear the shame” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 34:29 ('neither bear the shame of the heathen any more'), which supplies the whole five-word run 'bear the shame of the'.
provenance.significance: Jacob has run the two through each other and reversed both. Hebrews 12:2 has Christ enduring the cross and DESPISING the shame; Jacob asks the reader to 'suffer his cross, and bear the shame of the world' — the same pair, transferred from Christ to the disciple, with despising turned into bearing. Ezekiel 34:29 is a promise that a restored people will never again bear the shame of the heathen; Jacob asks his people to take up the shame of the world voluntarily. The borrowing is doing theological work in both directions: what Christ despised the disciple carries, and what the shepherd-oracle promised to lift off Israel is picked back up on purpose.
provenance.alternative: Matthew 16:24's 'take up his cross, and follow me' is the more familiar source for a cross laid on the disciple, and 'suffer his cross' may be no more than that; what Matthew has not got is the shame.

1:8.note: 'That all men would believe in Christ, and view his death, and suffer his cross, and bear the shame of the world.' The KJV joins a cross to a shame in exactly one verse, Hebrews 12:2, and Jacob has the pair in Hebrews' order while taking the words 'bear the shame of the' from the only KJV verse that contains them, Ezekiel 34:29. Moderate rather than high: neither source is reproduced as a clause, and the composite reading is this catalogue's proposal.
1:8.text: Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God.

provenance.other: “man to be a ruler over” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Chronicles 6:5: 'neither chose I any man to be a ruler over my people Israel'. Jacob 1:9 reads 'he anointed a man to be a king and a ruler over his people' — the singleton with two words inserted and the pronoun turned from 'my' to 'his'. “ruler over his people” occurs in no KJV verse at all; “ruler over my people” occurs in exactly four (2 Samuel 7:8, 1 Chronicles 11:2, 1 Chronicles 17:7, 2 Chronicles 6:5), and all four are about David.
provenance.significance: The one KJV sentence about appointing a man to be a ruler over the people is spoken by Solomon, at the dedication of the temple, and its content is a refusal: God chose no city and no man until he chose David and Jerusalem. Jacob 1:9 uses it for the moment the Nephites acquire a monarchy; Jacob 1:15 records what the monarchy immediately produced, 'such as like unto David of Old, desiring many wives and concubines, and also Solomon, his son'; and Jacob 1:17 has Jacob preaching against it in the temple. The chapter borrows the words of Solomon's temple prayer to install a king, and eight verses later is standing in a temple denouncing the people for imitating Solomon.

1:9.note: 'Wherefore, he anointed a man to be a king and a ruler over his people now, according to the reigns of the kings.' The phrase 'man to be a ruler over' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the two words Jacob inserts into it ('a king and') are the point of the sentence — 2 Chronicles 6:5 concerns choosing a ruler, and Jacob's people are getting a king. The anointing itself is the Samuel formula (1 Samuel 9:16, 'thou shalt anoint him to be captain over my people'), for which Jacob substitutes the Chronicler's noun.
1:9.text: Since the day that I brought forth my people out of the land of Egypt I chose no city among all the tribes of Israel to build an house in, that my name might be there; neither chose I any man to be a ruler over my people Israel:

provenance.mt: 1 Kings 11:3 — 'And he had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines: and his wives turned away his heart.'
provenance.route: 2 Samuel 5:13 + 1 Kings 11:1-3, against Deuteronomy 17:17 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “concubines and wives” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Samuel 5:13, and it is about David; Jacob 1:15 has the pair in the reverse order, 'many wives and concubines', which is no KJV string. The KJV never brings David's concubines and Solomon's wives into one sentence — 2 Samuel 5:13 and 1 Kings 11:1-3 are five centuries and eight books apart — and Jacob's pairing of the two is an act of reading, not of quotation.
provenance.significance: The law behind the complaint is Deuteronomy 17:17, the law of the king: 'Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away.' 1 Kings 11:3 reports the exact failure the law names — 'his wives turned away his heart' — and Jacob 1:15 reports it in a third nation, one verse after 'the second king' takes the throne and in the same breath as 'began to grow hard in their hearts'. The Nephite monarchy is being judged by the Deuteronomic law of the king within a verse of its founding, and Jacob 2 will make that judgment explicit.

1:15.note: 'Such as like unto David of Old, desiring many wives and concubines, and also Solomon, his son.' Hardy's cross-references here are 2 Samuel 5:13 and 1 Kings 11:1-3, and they are the right two: the KJV joins concubines to wives in exactly one verse, 2 Samuel 5:13, which is David's, and the seven hundred wives of 1 Kings 11:3 are Solomon's. What the Book of Mormon supplies is the conjunction of the two under a single charge, which the KJV nowhere makes and which Deuteronomy 17:17 licenses.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Jacob 1.15 (2 Samuel 5:13; 1 Kings 11:1-3)
1:15.text: And David took him more concubines and wives out of Jerusalem, after he was come from Hebron: and there were yet sons and daughters born to David.

provenance.other: “hardened in pride” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Daniel 5:20, which reads 'when his heart was lifted up, and his mind hardened in pride, he was deposed from his kingly throne'. That one verse contains both of the things Jacob 1:15-16 reports of the Nephites under their second king — a hardening and a lifting up in pride — in that order. “his heart was lifted up” occurs in exactly four KJV verses (2 Chronicles 17:6, 2 Chronicles 26:16, 2 Chronicles 32:25, Daniel 5:20), all of kings. “lifted up with pride” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Timothy 3:6, of a novice made an officer.
provenance.significance: Daniel 5:20 is the KJV's compressed account of what royal pride costs: Nebuchadnezzar's heart lifted up, his mind hardened in pride, deposed from his kingly throne. Jacob 1:15-16 narrates the same two motions in the same order under the reign of the second Nephite king, and Jacob 1:17 is the prophet arriving in the temple to preach against it — which is the office Daniel holds in his chapter. The alternative source is not idle either: 1 Timothy 3:6 warns against ordaining a novice 'lest being lifted up with pride he fall', and Jacob 1:18 is about who has been consecrated priest and by whose hand.
provenance.alternative: The vocabulary of a lifted-up heart is spread across four KJV verses and the whole prophetic idiom of pride; taken by itself 'lifted up somewhat in pride' identifies nothing. The case is the pairing with the hardening of 1:15.

1:16.note: 'They also began to search much gold and silver, and began to be lifted up somewhat in pride.' Read with 1:15's 'began to grow hard in their hearts', this is Daniel 5:20's two clauses in Daniel's order, and the KJV joins a hardening to a lifting-up in pride in that one verse only. Moderate: Jacob's preposition is 'in pride' where Daniel has 'in pride' of the mind and 1 Timothy 3:6 has 'with pride' of a man, and neither source is reproduced as a clause. The hardening at 1:15 is also doing double duty — it answers the 'harden not your hearts' of 1:7's Hebrews 3:8, and the chapter is arguably reporting the failure of its own opening warning.
1:16.text: But when his heart was lifted up, and his mind hardened in pride, he was deposed from his kingly throne, and they took his glory from him:

provenance.other: “magnify mine office” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 11:13. “mine office” itself occurs in exactly two (Genesis 41:13, of Pharaoh's butler restored, and Romans 11:13), and only Paul magnifies one. Jacob 1:19 reads 'we did magnify our office unto the Lord', the singleton put into the first person plural.
provenance.significance: The clause Jacob borrows is the hinge of Romans 11: Paul magnifies his office as apostle to the Gentiles precisely in order to 'provoke to emulation them which are my flesh, and might save some of them' — the office is magnified toward the salvation of Israel, at the writer's own risk. Jacob magnifies his in the same shape and spells out the risk in the same sentence: the sins of the people come upon his own head if he does not teach them. Paul's next verses are the olive tree and the branches broken off, which is the figure Jacob 5 will take over whole and run for seventy-seven verses. The one Pauline clause about magnifying an office arrives in the Book of Mormon four chapters before the allegory that stands beside it in Romans.

1:19.note: 'And we did magnify our office unto the Lord, taking upon us the responsibility.' A three-word KJV singleton, moved from Paul's first person singular to the first person plural of Jacob and Joseph. The verb is not a general one in the KJV — what is usually magnified is the Lord, or his law, or his word — and an office is magnified in exactly one verse.
1:19.text: For I speak to you Gentiles, inasmuch as I am the apostle of the Gentiles, I magnify mine office:

provenance.route: Acts 18:6 + Acts 20:26, over Ezekiel 33:1-9 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “our own heads” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 18:6 — 'Your blood be upon your own heads; I am clean' — where it is 'your'. “pure from the blood” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 20:26, Paul's farewell at Miletus: 'I take you to record this day, that I am pure from the blood of all men.' Jacob 1:19 has both halves of Paul's formula, the blood and the cleanness of the preacher, and takes the heads onto himself: the sins of the people come 'upon our own heads' if the teaching fails.
provenance.significance: The reversal is the finding. Paul says the blood is on THEIR heads and he is clean; Jacob says it will be on OURS if we do not teach. The Old Testament source behind Paul is the watchman of Ezekiel 33:6, whose failure to blow the trumpet makes him answerable — 'his blood will I require at the watchman's hand' — and Jacob has restored Ezekiel's liability to Paul's wording. What the two testaments hold apart, the verse fuses: Acts supplies the phrase, Ezekiel supplies the direction, and the result is a consecrated priest who is not clean by default.
provenance.alternative: The image of blood on a garment is also Isaiah 63:3 and Revelation 19:13, but those are the treader of the winepress and are stained on purpose; nothing in them concerns a teacher's liability.

1:19.note: 'Answering the sins of the people upon our own heads, if we did not teach them the word of God with all diligence; wherefore, by laboring with our mights, their blood might not come upon our garments.' Two KJV singletons stand behind the sentence, 'our own heads' at Acts 18:6 and 'pure from the blood' at Acts 20:26, both of them Paul disclaiming responsibility for hearers who would not listen. Jacob keeps the words and inverts the claim, which is Ezekiel 33:6's watchman rather than Paul's shaken raiment. The garments are Jacob's own contribution: no KJV verse puts a hearer's blood on a teacher's clothes.
1:19.text: And when they opposed themselves, and blasphemed, he shook his raiment, and said unto them, Your blood be upon your own heads; I am clean; from henceforth I will go unto the Gentiles.

provenance.other: “the sins of the people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 2:17: 'that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make reconciliation for the sins of the people'. Jacob 1:18-19 is about two men 'consecrated priests' who take the sins of the people upon their own heads.
provenance.significance: The one KJV verse that speaks of the sins of the people speaks of a high priest who bears them, and Jacob's sentence is written by a consecrated priest describing what he does with them. Read with the Hebrews 3 that governs Jacob 1:7, the borrowing is not isolated: Hebrews 2:17 is eight verses before 3:1's 'consider the Apostle and High Priest of our profession', and this chapter has already followed Hebrews 3 down to 3:18. The chapter's two ends, the exhortation at 1:7 and the priesthood at 1:19, are drawn from the same three columns of the epistle.
provenance.alternative: 'The sins of the people' is an obvious enough thing for a priest to say and the collocation is common in the Levitical vocabulary generally (Leviticus 4:3, 'the sin of the people'); the singleton is a fact about the exact string, not about the idea.

1:19.note: 'Answering the sins of the people upon our own heads.' The phrase occurs in exactly one KJV verse and that verse defines the office Jacob 1:18 has just claimed. Catalogued as an echo, not an allusion: four words shared, no syntax carried over, and the case rests on the coincidence of the wording with the priesthood the previous verse establishes and with the run through Hebrews 3 that the chapter has already made at 1:7.
1:19.text: Wherefore in all things it behoved him to be made like unto his brethren, that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make reconciliation for the sins of the people.

provenance.other: “be found of him in peace” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Peter 3:14, which continues 'without spot, and blameless' — the KJV's one place where being FOUND and being without spot are joined, and where the finding is eschatological (the verse before it is the new heavens and new earth). Jacob 1:19 reads 'we would not be found spotless at the last day'. “at the last day” occurs in exactly five KJV verses, all of them in John (6:39, 6:40, 6:44, 6:54, 11:24), so the temporal clause is Johannine and the spotlessness is Petrine.
provenance.significance: Jacob's closing clause is a composite of the two KJV idioms for the end: John's day on which the dead are raised, and Peter's inspection at which the diligent are found without spot. What Peter asks of every reader — 'be diligent that ye may be found of him in peace, without spot' — Jacob makes conditional on an office: he will be found spotless only if he has taught with diligence, and the same word does the work in both. Jude 1:23's 'garment spotted by the flesh' stands behind the metaphor's other half, since Jacob's spot is on a garment stained by someone else's blood.

1:19.note: 'Otherwise, their blood would come upon our garments, and we would not be found spotless at the last day.' Two KJV formulas are welded here: 'found … without spot' from 2 Peter 3:14, the only verse joining them, and 'at the last day', which occurs in exactly five KJV verses and all of them are John's. Moderate, and an echo rather than an allusion, because neither phrase is reproduced intact — 'found spotless' compresses Peter's three words into one.
1:19.text: Wherefore, beloved, seeing that ye look for such things, be diligent that ye may be found of him in peace, without spot, and blameless.
